'''Federico Cafiero''' (24 May 1914 – 7 May 1980) was an Italian mathematician known for his contributions in [[real analysis]], [[measure theory|measure]] and [[Integral (mathematics)|integration theory]], and in the theory of [[ordinary differential equation]]s. In particular, generalizing the [[Vitali convergence theorem]], the [[Fichera convergence theorem]] and previous results of [[Vladimir Mikhailovich Dubrovskii]], he proved a necessary and sufficient condition for the passage to the [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]] under the sign of [[Integral (mathematics)|integral]]:<ref>See {{harv|Cafiero|1953}}, {{harv|Cafiero|1953a}} and {{harv|Cafiero|1959|pp=388–392}}.</ref> this result is, in some sense, definitive.<ref>According to {{harvtxt|Letta|1981|pp=353–354}}.</ref> In the field of ordinary differential equations, he studied existence and uniqueness problems under very general hypotheses for the left member of the given first-order equation, developing an important approximation method and proving a fundamental uniqueness theorem.<ref>According to {{harvtxt|Letta|1981|pp=349–350}}, who describes briefly these results, and to {{harvtxt|Piccinini|Stampacchia|Vidossich|1978}}, who comprehensively present Cafiero's and other's research results in this field.</ref>

==Life and academic career==

Cafiero was born in [[Riposto]], [[Province of Catania]], on May 24, 1914.<ref>See {{harv|Letta|1981|p=347}} and {{harv|Miranda|1980–1981|p=9}}: his parents were from [[Meta di Sorrento]], according to Miranda.</ref> He obtained his [[Laurea]] in mathematics, [[cum laude]], from the [[University of Naples Federico II]] in 1939.<ref name="Letta347">See {{harv|Letta|1981|p=347}}.</ref> During the 1939–1940 [[academic year]], he won an  "[[Istituto Nazionale di Alta Matematica]]" scholarship and went in Rome to the institute:<ref>See {{harv|Letta|1981|p=347}}, {{harv|Miranda|1980–1981|p=9}} and {{harv|Roghi|2005|p=13}}: Letta and Roghi clearly state the academic year, while Miranda states that he won the scholarship "''subito dopo''" i.e. "''soon after''" earning his Laurea degree. Roghi gives many other details about the scholarship, including the names of other winners and its amount, which was 5000 [[Italian lira]]s.</ref> there he followed the courses held by [[Francesco Severi]], [[Mauro Picone]], [[Luigi Fantappiè]], [[Giulio Krall]] and [[Leonida Tonelli]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Miranda|1980–1981|p=9}} lists only the first four names while {{harvtxt|Letta|1981|p=347}} also mentions Tonelli but not Krall. {{harvtxt|Roghi|2005|p=13}} gives the full list of the courses held at the institute during the 1939–1940 academic year, including the names of the appointed teachers: along with the ones cited by Letta and Miranda, [[Enrico Bompiani]], [[Giovanni Giorgi]], [[Ugo Amaldi (mathematician)|Ugo Amaldi]], [[Antonio Signorini (physicist)|Antonio Signorini]] and [[Fabio Conforto]] are also mentioned.</ref>

===World War II years: 1941–1943===

He was appointed instructor of the course of "Elementi di matematica"<ref>English translation: "Elements of mathematics".</ref> by the Faculty of Statistical Sciences of the University of Rome, for the 1940–1941 academic year:<ref>According to {{harvtxt|Letta|1981|p=347}}, who reports also that Cafiero was confirmed in the job for the three following years. {{harvtxt|Miranda|1980–1981|p=9}} presents a slightly different version, referring that he was appointed instructor of the course of "Esercitazioni di Matematiche" (i.e. "Exercises in mathematics") by the Faculty of sciences. However, the version of Letta has been followed since it is more circumstantial, offering more details.</ref> however, he was able to hold the course only for a few months, since he was called to arms in January 1941<ref name="Le347Mir9" >See {{harv|Letta|1981|p=347}} and {{harv|Miranda|1980–1981|p=9}}.</ref> and stationed from May 1942 to September 1943 on the Northern African coasts as an [[officer]] of the [[San Marco Regiment|San Marco Battalion]].<ref>See {{harv|Letta|1981|p=347}} and {{harv|Miranda|1980–1981|p=9}}: unlike the former one, this last source does not state the duration of Cafiero's stay in Africa.</ref> It was there that, after having successfully completed a dangerous [[sabotage]] operation, the [[Armistice between Italy and Allied armed forces]] surprised him and the other members of his unit, leaving them without any support.<ref name="Le347Mir9" /> Nonetheless, in desperate conditions, he was able to lead his men to the [[Italia]]n coasts with a [[rubber]] [[dinghy]], and was awarded a [[Silver Medal of Military Valor]] for this act.<ref name="Le347Mir9" />

===Rebuilding and researching: the years 1944–1953===
After being discharged from [[Military Service]] in February 1944,<ref name="Letta347" /> he remained in Naples.<ref name="Le347Mir9" />

The Institute of Mathematics of the University of Naples was in the process of reconstituting<ref>Description of the state the Institute at the time, as reported here, is taken from the brief but vivid description given by {{harvtxt|Miranda|1980–1981|p=9}}.</ref> as the eight former mathematics institutes of the university was literally "torn to pieces" by the [[Allies of World War II|Allied forces]] [[Military Police]].<ref name="Mir9">See {{harv|Miranda|1980–1981|p=9}}.</ref>

Reconstitution consisted of collecting and reordering all the volumes of the previously existing library, then piled on the floor of a single room, catalogue them [[ex novo]] and create new records and provide the library administration for the new library as there was no administrative personnel available nor financial resources.<ref>{{harvtxt|Miranda|1980–1981|p=9}} remarks precisely that, to perform all those tasks, they could only rely on two old janitors, and that the funds available for the institution were trifling.</ref>

work was done to organize courses and exams for the numerous war veterans coming back from the front and for new students, with more than a half of the teaching personnel blocked beyond the [[Gothic Line]]:<ref name="Mir9" /> and in performing all those task Cafiero, jointly with few others and working as an adjunct professor of "Esercitazioni di Matematiche", was a collaborator of [[Renato Caccioppoli]] and [[Carlo Miranda]].<ref>This highly positive assessment of his work during those years is due to {{harvtxt|Miranda|1980–1981|p=9}} himself.</ref>

Also in 1944 he married Jole Giorgini, his lifelong companion, and soon after they had a daughter, Anna.<ref name="Letta347" />

Due to the scarce possibilities of being hired permanently by the Faculty of Sciences at that time, he accepted a position as adjunct [[assistant professor]] to the chair of [[Financial Mathematics]],<ref>For the academic year 1944/45, according to {{harvtxt|De Angelis|Sbordone|1999|p=29}}.</ref> working with Luigi Lordi first at the [[Istituto Universitario Navale]] and then to the Faculty of Economics and Business, where he was appointed full [[assistant professor]] in June 1949.<ref>{{harvtxt|Miranda|1980–1981|p=9}} details briefly but comprehensively these early career steps, while {{harvtxt|Letta|1981|p=347}} only outlines them. {{harvtxt|De Angelis|Sbordone|1999|p=29}} state precisely the academic years and the course held by Cafiero at the Institute.</ref> Nonetheless, his ties with the Faculty of Sciences remained strong, being employed there as an adjunct professor of "Esercitazioni di Matematiche" several times, during those years:<ref name="Mir10" >See {{harv|Miranda|1980–1981|p=10}}.</ref> he was likewise assigned to several other courses related to Financial Mathematics by the Istituto Universitario Navale and by the Faculty of Business and Economics.<ref name="Mir10" /><ref>{{harvtxt|De Angelis|Sbordone|1999|p=29}} state that he was a lecturer (the exact Italian academic rank was "professore incaricato") of "Matematica generale" (Free English translation:"General mathematics") for the academic year 1952/1953.</ref>

The scientific aspect of the collaboration with the Faculty of Sciences was nonetheless very intense,<ref name="Mir10" /> leading him to the "libera docenza" in March 1951, and to a full professorship chair in 1953:<ref>The "''free  professorship''" (in a literal free English translation) was an academic title similar to the [[Habilitation#Germany|German "Habilitation"]], no longer in force in Italy since 1970.</ref><ref name="Le347Mir10" >See {{harvtxt|Letta|1981|p=347}} and {{harv|Miranda|1980–1981|p=10}}.</ref> during this period, his scientific activity was done side by side at first with Carlo Miranda and later with Renato Caccioppoli, who found in him a dear pupil and friend.<ref>See {{harv|Miranda|1980–1981|p=10}}: Miranda precisely uses the term "''carissimo''", which in the Italian language means more than ''dear'' (caro) and less than ''dearest'' (il più caro).</ref>

Ranked first of the three winners of the competition for the chair of [[mathematical analysis]] of the [[University of Catania]],<ref>See the announce on the [[#{{harvid|UMI|1954}}|Bollettino UMI (1953]], p. 471), reporting also the names of other winners and of the judging committee.</ref> in December 1953 he was appointed as [[extraordinary professor]] to that chair, and left Naples for Catania.<ref>See {{harvtxt|Letta|1981|p=347}}, {{harv|Miranda|1980–1981|p=10}} and the announce on the [[#{{harvid|UMI|1954}}|Bollettino UMI (1953]], p. 472),  "Nomine di nuovi professori straordinari" section: Letta and Miranda precisely state the month and the year of his appointment.</ref><ref name="teach">See also the "[[#Teaching activity|Teaching activity]]" section.</ref>

===First in Catania and then in Pisa: the years 1954–1959===

Cafiero started his service at the University of Catania in January 1954.<ref>See {{harv|Letta|1981|p=347}}, {{harv|Marino|2008|p=2}}, {{harv|Maugeri|1994|p=179}} and {{harv|Miranda|1980–1981|p=10}}. Letta, Maugeri and Miranda precisely state the month and the year of his arrival: on the other hand, Maugeri and Marino refer also that he substituted Vincenzo Amato (1881–1963), retired during the [[academic year]] 1951–1952.</ref> His arrival at the university brought several innovations, both in teaching and in the research activity on [[mathematical analysis]].<ref name="teach" /><ref name="Mau179">According to {{harvtxt|Maugeri|1994|p=179}} and to {{harvtxt|Marino|2013|pp=93–94}}, who reports a piece of an address by [[Francesco Guglielmino]].</ref> In particular, he established a [[seminar]] on abstract measure theory open to assistant professors and to graduate students as well, and this was felt as true scientific revolution:<ref name="Mau179" /> he held the chair of mathematical analysis for three years.<ref>See {{harv|Letta|1981|p=347}} and {{harv|Miranda|1980–1981|p=11}}. Letta precisely states that the 1955/1956 academic year was his last one in Catania.</ref> After becoming [[ordinary professor]] in 1956,<ref name="Letta347" /> he went to the [[University of Pisa]] on request by [[Sandro Faedo]]:<ref>As Faedo himself briefly recalls in {{Harv|Faedo|1986|p=104}}.</ref> during his stay, he held courses also at the [[Scuola Normale Superiore]],<ref>See {{harv|Letta|1981|p=348}} and {{harv|Miranda|1980–1981|p=11}}.</ref> becoming director of the "''[[Leonida Tonelli]]''" Institute and member of [[Board of directors]] of the [[Centro Studi Calcolatrici Elettroniche]].<ref>According to {{harvtxt|Letta|1981|p=348}}, who refers also that he was awarded a gold medal for the role he played in the construction of a new [[electronic computer]] at the university.</ref>

===Honors===
Apart from the silver medal awarded him for his valor acts during the military service,<ref name="Le347Mir9" /> the importance of his scientific achievements was acknowledged several times. 
In 1952 he received the Tenore Prize of the Accademia Pontaniana for a memoir on the theory of integration,<ref name="PontPrize"/> later published as the paper {{harv|Cafiero|1953}} and the monograph {{harv|Cafiero|1953a}}. On May 25, 1954 he was elected ''resident corresponding member'' of the [[Accademia Gioenia di Catania]] during his stay at the University of Catania, and became ''non resident corresponding member'' from November 16, 1956 on, after his moving to Pisa and then to Naples.<ref name="MauSpa19">According to {{harvtxt|Marino|Spampinato|2018|p=19}}.</ref>

==Work==

===Research activity===

{{blockquote
|text= Ma è subito dopo la seconda guerra mondiale che il ''processo di astrattizzazione'' della teoria della misura e dell'integrale si completa in modo definitivo. A ciò contribuirono [[Paul Halmos]] negli U.S.A. e [[Renato Caccioppoli]], Federico Cafiero (1914–1980) ed altri in Italia.<ref>(English translation) "But it was immediately after the second world war that the ''process of abstraction'' of measure and integration theory was completed in a definitive manner. Paul Halmos in the U.S.A. and Renato Caccioppoli, Federico Cafiero (1914–1980) and others in Italy were the main contributors". The [[Italic type]] emphasis is due to the Author himself.</ref>
|sign= [[Gaetano Fichera]] 
|source= {{Harv|Fichera|1993|p=78}}.
}}

===Teaching activity===

{{blockquote
|text= Come [[Aldo Andreotti|Andreotti]] anche [[Guido Stampacchia|Stampacchia]] non poté venire subito a Pisa e così io fui felice di avere con me un altro valoroso allievo di Renato Caccioppoli, Federico Cafiero, che restò a Pisa poco tempo, ma vi lasciò una forte traccia e formò il suo valido continuatore Giorgio Letta.<ref>(English translation) "As Andreotti also Stampacchia could not come immediately to Pisa therefore I was happy to have with me another valiant pupil of Renato Caccioppoli, Federico Cafiero, who was in Pisa for a short time but left a strong trace and formed his valid successor Giorgio Letta."</ref>
|sign= [[Sandro Faedo]] 
|source= {{Harv|Faedo|1986|p=104}}.
}}

==Selected publications==

The papers of Federico Cafiero listed in this section are also included in his "''Opere scelte''" {{harv|Cafiero|1996}}, which collects all his published notes and one of his books. 
*{{Citation
|last = Cafiero
|first = Federico
|title = Sul passaggio al limite sotto il segno d'integrale per successioni d'integrali di Stieltjes-Lebesgue negli spazi astratti, con masse variabili con gli integrandi
|trans-title=On the passage to the limit under the sign of integral for sequences of Stieltjes–Lebesgue integrals in abstract spaces, with masses varying jointly with integrands
|journal = [[Rendiconti del Seminario Matematico della Università di Padova]]
|volume = 22
|pages = 223–245
|year = 1953
|language = it
|url = http://www.numdam.org/item?id=RSMUP_1953__22__223_0
|mr = 57951
|zbl = 0052.05003
}}, is the first paper where Federico Cafiero states and proves his convergence theorem.
*{{Citation
|last = Cafiero
|first = Federico
|title = Funzioni additive d'insieme e integrazione negli spazi astratti
|trans-title=Additive set functions and integration in abstract spaces
|place = [[Naples]]
|publisher = [[Liguori Editore|Libreria Editrice Liguori]]
|year = 1953a
|pages = 178
|mr = 0056671
|zbl = 0050.27801
|language = it
}}, is the prize-winning first monograph where Federico Cafiero states and proves his convergence theorem.
*{{Citation
|last = Cafiero
|first = Federico
|title = Misura e integrazione
|trans-title=Measure and integration
|place = [[Rome]]
|publisher = Edizioni Cremonese
|year = 1959
|series = Monografie matematiche del [[Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche]]
|volume = 5
|pages = VII+451
|mr = 0215954 
|zbl = 0171.01503
|language = it
|url=https://archive.org/embed/consiglionaziona0005fede
}}, is a definitive monograph on integration and measure theory: the treatment of the limiting behaviour of the integral of various kinds of [[sequences]] of measure-related structures (measurable functions, [[measurable set]]s, measures and their combinations) is somewhat conclusive.
*{{Citation
|last = Cafiero
|first = Federico
|title = Opere scelte
|place = [[Naples]]
|publisher = [[Giannini Editore]]
|series = a cura del Dipartimento di matematica e applicazioni R. Caccioppoli dell'Università degli studi di Napoli Federico II e con il contributo dell'Accademia Pontaniana e dei dipartimenti di matematica delle università di Catania, di Napoli e di Pisa
|year = 1996
|pages = 701
|language = it
}}. Federico Cafiero's "''Selected works''", including all his published papers, three postcards from his master Renato Caccioppoli concerning his research and his book "''Lezioni sulla teoria delle funzioni di variabili reali''" ({{langx|en|italic=yes|"Lectures on the theory of functions of real variables")}}.

This is a [[monograph]]ic [[Serial (literature)|fascicle]] published on the "Bollettino della Unione Matematica Italiana", describing the history of the "Istituto Nazionale di Alta Matematica Francesco Severi" from its foundation in 1939 to 2003. It was written by Gino Roghi and includes a presentation by Salvatore Coen and a preface by [[Corrado De Concini]]. It is almost exclusively based on [[source text|sources]] from the institute archives: the wealth and variety of materials included, jointly with its [[Addendum#In books|appendices]] and [[Index (publishing)|indexes]], make this monograph a useful reference not only for the history of the [[institute]] itself, but also for the history of many [[mathematician]]s who taught or followed the institute courses or simply worked there.
